warmup.q: The clerk's rules are written as a switch, in this order: case Book b when b.newRelease() -> 7;, then case Book b when b.format() == LARGE_PRINT -> 42;, then case Book b -> 21;. How many days does a new large-print book get?
options: 42, because the more specific rule wins
7, because cases are tried from the top and the first match wins
It doesn't compile: two guarded cases for the same type are ambiguous
It doesn't compile: the large-print case is dominated by the new-release case
warmup.why: Java tries the cases in order and runs the first one whose pattern matches and whose guard is true. Both guards are true for a new large-print book, so the new-release rule wins. javac doesn't compare guards, so it can't tell that the large-print rule is shadowed for new releases: a guarded case never dominates another. Put the large-print rule first, as the section on guards shows.

opening:
At the lending desk, a clerk picks up each item a member wants to borrow, looks at it once, and stamps a due date. A large-print book gets six weeks. A new release gets one week, because other people are waiting for it. A box set of DVDs gets two. One look tells the clerk what kind of item it is and reads the stickers on its label too. The clerk works down a printed instruction sheet, and the first line that fits wins.

Java code used to sort things the slow way: instanceof, a cast, a getter, then another instanceof. It works, and it hides two traps. Nothing checks that the chain covers every kind of item, and nothing checks that a line further down can ever be reached.

Sealed types, in the last lesson, gave the compiler the complete list of kinds. In this lesson, we'll give that list to a clerk who can use it. We'll write a switch the compiler checks, read several boxes in one look with record patterns, let guards decide the order, and meet the odd things that happen with null. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the lending desk, with a clerk who reads each item in one look and works down a printed sheet. A pattern switch is that clerk. javac checks that the sheet covers every kind of item, record patterns read the boxes inside each record, and the order of the guards is the order of the rules.

Now look in your own code for instanceof followed by a cast or a getter on the next line. Each one is a chain that a switch could check.

Next, we'll put records, sealed types and switches together into one way of designing programs. What does a program look like when the forms can't be filled in wrong?

sections.h: A pattern switch is checked, an instanceof chain is not
sections.html:
A pattern is a test with a binding. Book b asks "is this value a Book?" and, if it is, gives you a new variable b of type Book. Pattern matching came to Java in steps. JDK 16 made instanceof patterns a standard feature (JEP 394, the JDK Enhancement Proposal that describes them). The type test and the cast become one, and the binding is in scope wherever the test is known to have passed:

Java
if (!(o instanceof Book b)) return "not a book";
return "by " + b.author();               // b is in scope: the test can't have failed here
Kotlin
if (o !is Item.Book) return "not a book"
return "by ${o.author}"                  // smart cast: o is a Book from here on

JDK 21 made pattern switch standard (JEP 441), together with record patterns (JEP 440). Here are two ways to describe an item at the desk, both from the PatternBasics demo:

Java
// an if-chain: javac never checks that it covers every Item
if (i instanceof Book b) return "book " + b.title() + " by " + b.author();
else if (i instanceof Disc d) return "disc " + d.title() + ", " + d.minutes() + " min";
else if (i instanceof Magazine m) return "magazine " + m.title() + " #" + m.issue();
else throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable?");

// a pattern switch: javac checks that every Item is covered
return switch (i) {
    case Book b -> "book " + b.title() + " by " + b.author();
    case Disc d -> "disc " + d.title() + ", " + d.minutes() + " min";
    case Magazine m -> "magazine " + m.title() + " #" + m.issue();
};
Kotlin
// an if-chain: kotlinc never checks that it covers every Item
if (i is Item.Book) "book ${i.title} by ${i.author}"
else if (i is Item.Disc) "disc ${i.title}, ${i.minutes} min"
else if (i is Item.Magazine) "magazine ${i.title} #${i.issue}"
else throw IllegalStateException("unreachable?")

// when with a subject: kotlinc checks that every Item is covered
when (i) {
    is Item.Book -> "book ${i.title} by ${i.author}"
    is Item.Disc -> "disc ${i.title}, ${i.minutes} min"
    is Item.Magazine -> "magazine ${i.title} #${i.issue}"
}

Both print the same three lines, starting with book Emma by Jane Austen. It's tempting to read the switch as a tidier chain, but the differences are the reason to prefer it. Delete the Magazine line from the chain, and it still compiles; the run reaches the magazine and dies in the chain's IllegalStateException. Delete the Magazine case from the switch, and javac, the Java compiler, refuses: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. A pattern switch used as a statement must be exhaustive too.

javac checks two more things the chain never gets: dominance, that is, whether each case can ever be reached (the third section), and fixed rules for null (the fourth). One level down, javac compiles the switch to one invokedynamic call, a call whose target the JVM picks the first time the call runs, to SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch. That method works out the first matching case. javac also adds a hidden last arm that throws MatchException if nothing matches at run time. Hold on to that hidden arm; it comes back at the end of the lesson.

Kotlin has had most of this for years. A when with a subject checks exhaustiveness over a sealed type, whether you use it as an expression or a statement, and a smart cast merges the is check with the cast. javap, the JDK's class-file reader, shows that kotlinc 2.4 (the Kotlin compiler), with the JDK 21 target, compiles that when to the same typeSwitch call; its hidden arm throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException instead.

In the paperwork picture, the switch is a clerk whose printed sheet lists every kind of item the library has. The chain is a clerk who remembers the kinds. Mostly.

A chain of instanceof checks can't be checked. Switch over the sealed type instead.

What Kotlin doesn't have is the subject of the next section: reading the boxes inside the item, in the same look.

steps: Run PatternBasics (or PatternBasicsKt) with the command below.
Delete the Magazine line from viaChain and run. Put it back, then delete the Magazine case from viaSwitch and run again. Which mistake did the compiler catch?
From labs/, run javap -c -p modernjava/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasics.class and find typeSwitch and MatchException in viaSwitch.

code.title: PatternBasics.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** The same sorting three ways: an instanceof chain, an early return, and a pattern switch. */ public class PatternBasics { sealed interface Item permits Book, Disc, Magazine {} record Book(String title, String author) implements Item {} record Disc(String title, int minutes) implements Item {} record Magazine(String title, int issue) implements Item {} // an if-chain: javac never checks that it covers every Item static String viaChain(Item i) { if (i instanceof Book b) return "book " + b.title() + " by " + b.author(); else if (i instanceof Disc d) return "disc " + d.title() + ", " + d.minutes() + " min"; else if (i instanceof Magazine m) return "magazine " + m.title() + " #" + m.issue(); else throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable?"); } // a pattern switch: javac checks that every Item is covered static String viaSwitch(Item i) { return switch (i) { case Book b -> "book " + b.title() + " by " + b.author(); case Disc d -> "disc " + d.title() + ", " + d.minutes() + " min"; case Magazine m -> "magazine " + m.title() + " #" + m.issue(); }; } // flow scoping: after the negated test returns, b is in scope for the rest of the method static String author(Object o) { if (!(o instanceof Book b)) return "not a book"; return "by " + b.author(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Item[] returns = { new Book("Emma", "Jane Austen"), new Disc("Paddington", 95), new Magazine("Garden Monthly", 214) }; for (Item i : returns) { System.out.println(viaChain(i) + " | " + viaSwitch(i)); } System.out.println(author(returns[0]) + ", " + author("Emma")); } }

alt.title: PatternBasics.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo sealed interface Item { data class Book(val title: String, val author: String) : Item data class Disc(val title: String, val minutes: Int) : Item data class Magazine(val title: String, val issue: Int) : Item } // an if-chain: kotlinc never checks that it covers every Item fun viaChain(i: Item): String = if (i is Item.Book) "book ${i.title} by ${i.author}" // smart cast: i is a Book here else if (i is Item.Disc) "disc ${i.title}, ${i.minutes} min" else if (i is Item.Magazine) "magazine ${i.title} #${i.issue}" else throw IllegalStateException("unreachable?") // when with a subject: kotlinc checks that every Item is covered fun viaWhen(i: Item): String = when (i) { is Item.Book -> "book ${i.title} by ${i.author}" is Item.Disc -> "disc ${i.title}, ${i.minutes} min" is Item.Magazine -> "magazine ${i.title} #${i.issue}" } // a smart cast lasts for the rest of the function after a negated check returns fun author(o: Any): String { if (o !is Item.Book) return "not a book" return "by ${o.author}" } /** The same sorting three ways: an if-chain, an early return, and a when. */ fun main() { val returns = listOf(Item.Book("Emma", "Jane Austen"), Item.Disc("Paddington", 95), Item.Magazine("Garden Monthly", 214)) for (i in returns) { println(viaChain(i) + " | " + viaWhen(i)) } println(author(returns[0]) + ", " + author("Emma")) }

try.expect: Both versions print the same three lines and by Jane Austen, not a book. Without its Magazine branch the chain still compiles, and the run crashes on the magazine with the chain's IllegalStateException. Without its Magazine case the switch doesn't compile: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (kotlinc: Add the 'is Magazine' branch or an 'else' branch.). In the bytecode, viaSwitch has invokedynamic ... typeSwitch and new java/lang/MatchException; the Kotlin viaWhen has the same typeSwitch call and new kotlin/NoWhenBranchMatchedException.

sections.h: Record patterns read several boxes in one look
sections.html:
A type pattern tests a type and binds one variable. A record pattern also takes a record apart, through its accessors, and each part can be a pattern too. In the picture, the clerk reads several boxes in one look, including the boxes on a smaller form clipped inside the first.

The lab's loan rules show it. A Loan records who borrows (a Member), what (an Item), and from which branch (a Branch, where BUS is the library bus that comes back every four weeks). Here are the first rules, next to the closest Kotlin. The when after each pattern is a guard, an extra condition that the next section covers:

Java
return switch (loan) {
    case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42;
    case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when isNew -> 7;
    case Loan(var m, Book book, var b) when b == Branch.BUS -> 28;
    // ...
};
Kotlin
val item = loan.item                         // pick the nested part out first
return when (item) {
    is Book if item.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42
    is Book if item.newRelease -> 7
    is Book if loan.branch == Branch.BUS -> 28
    // ...
}

Read the Java label from the outside in. The selector, the value in switch (...), must be a Loan. Its member() binds to m. Its item() must match Book(var format, var isNew), which binds the book's two boxes. Its branch() binds to b. With var, javac infers each type from the record's components. The figure shows one pattern that reads every box at once, three levels deep.

Patterns are positional and type-checked. Put String x2 where a record has an int, as the Try it does, and javac stops with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. Generic records work too: over sealed interface Result<T>, the case Ok<T>(var v) binds v as a T. Record patterns also work in instanceof, as in if (o instanceof Line(Point(var x, var y), var to) && x == 0).

Kotlin has no record patterns. The closest tools are smart casts on nested properties, as in the twin above, and positional destructuring, val (from, to) = line, through component1() and component2(). Destructuring has a trap that Java's patterns mostly avoid: it goes by position, not by name. With data class Book(val title: String, val pages: Int), the line val (pages, title) = book compiles without a warning. The demo prints swapped names: pages=Dune title=412, a very long book with a very short title.

Kotlin 2.3.20 added name-based destructuring as an Experimental feature, behind -Xname-based-destructuring; its name-mismatch mode warns about exactly that line. Java's record patterns are positional too, but every component is type-checked, so most swaps fail to compile. Two var bindings of the same type can still be swapped silently, so keep the record header in front of you.

One look now reads every box. The clerk still needs to know which line of the sheet to try first.

try.title: Take a line apart
steps: Predict the third line of output, then run RecordPatterns.
In describe, change Point(int x2, int y2) to Point(String x2, int y2) and run. Read the first error, then undo it.
Run the Kotlin twin, RecordPatternsKt, and read its last line.

code.title: RecordPatterns.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; import java.util.List; /** Record patterns: take a record apart in the case label, nested as deep as you like. */ public class RecordPatterns { record Point(int x, int y) {} record Line(Point from, Point to) {} sealed interface Result<T> permits Ok, Err {} record Ok<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {} record Err<T>(String message, Throwable cause) implements Result<T> {} static String describe(Line line) { return switch (line) { case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(int x2, int y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical at x=" + x1 + " len " + Math.abs(y2 - y1); case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when y1 == y2 -> "horizontal at y=" + y1; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "diagonal " + from + "->" + to; }; } static <T> String show(Result<T> r) { return switch (r) { case Ok<T>(var v) -> "ok " + v; // T inferred for v case Err<T>(var msg, var cause) when cause != null -> "err " + msg + " caused by " + cause.getClass().getSimpleName(); case Err<T>(var msg, var cause) -> "err " + msg; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(1, 0), new Point(1, 5)))); System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(0, 3), new Point(7, 3)))); System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(0, 0), new Point(2, 2)))); System.out.println(show(new Ok<>(List.of(1, 2)))); System.out.println(show(new Err<>("boom", new RuntimeException()))); Object o = new Line(new Point(0, 0), new Point(9, 9)); if (o instanceof Line(Point(var x, var y), var to) && x == 0 && y == 0) { // patterns in instanceof too System.out.println("from origin to " + to); } } }

alt.title: RecordPatterns.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) data class Line(val from: Point, val to: Point) sealed interface Outcome<out T> { data class Ok<T>(val value: T) : Outcome<T> data class Err(val message: String, val cause: Throwable?) : Outcome<Nothing> } data class Book(val title: String, val pages: Int) // Kotlin can't take records apart in a when branch: match the outer type, then read the properties fun describe(line: Line): String { val (from, to) = line // positional destructuring via component1/2 return when { from.x == to.x -> "vertical at x=${from.x} len ${kotlin.math.abs(to.y - from.y)}" from.y == to.y -> "horizontal at y=${from.y}" else -> "diagonal $from->$to" } } fun <T> show(r: Outcome<T>): String = when (r) { is Outcome.Ok -> "ok ${r.value}" is Outcome.Err if r.cause != null -> "err ${r.message} caused by ${r.cause::class.simpleName}" // guard: Kotlin 2.2+ is Outcome.Err -> "err ${r.message}" } /** The Kotlin side: smart casts and positional destructuring instead of record patterns. */ fun main() { println(describe(Line(Point(1, 0), Point(1, 5)))) println(describe(Line(Point(0, 3), Point(7, 3)))) println(describe(Line(Point(0, 0), Point(2, 2)))) println(show(Outcome.Ok(listOf(1, 2)))) println(show(Outcome.Err("boom", RuntimeException()))) val o: Any = Line(Point(0, 0), Point(9, 9)) if (o is Line && o.from.x == 0 && o.from.y == 0) { // smart cast after the is check println("from origin to ${o.to}") } // destructuring goes by position, not by name: this compiles, with no warning, and swaps the values val (pages, title) = Book("Dune", 412) println("swapped names: pages=$pages title=$title") }

try.expect: vertical at x=1 len 5, horizontal at y=3, diagonal Point[x=0, y=0]->Point[x=2, y=2], then ok [1, 2], err boom caused by RuntimeException and from origin to Point[x=9, y=9]. The String change fails with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String (and a second error, because x1 == x2 now compares an int with a String). The Kotlin twin prints the same results with smart casts, and then swapped names: pages=Dune title=412: positional destructuring put the title into pages without a warning.

sections.h: Guards, order and dominance: the sheet is read from the top
sections.html:
Cases are tried from the top, and the first one whose pattern matches and whose guard is true wins. The guard is the when clause after a pattern (if in Kotlin). That makes order part of the meaning, exactly as on the clerk's sheet. A new large-print book matches both of the first two lines of the GuardsDemo, so whichever comes first sets its loan:

Java
case Book(var format, var isNew) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42;   // 1
case Book(var format, var isNew) when isNew -> 7;                          // 2
case Book(var format, var isNew) -> 21;                                    // 3
Kotlin
is LoanItem.Book if i.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42   // 1
is LoanItem.Book if i.newRelease -> 7                      // 2
is LoanItem.Book -> 21                                     // 3

The demo prints 42 days for it. Swap lines // 1 and // 2, and it prints 7 days, and nothing else changes. javac accepts both orders, because a guarded case never dominates another. Only a test that sends a new large-print book through the switch can tell you which order you meant.

Guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, in either language. The compiler can't prove that a set of guards covers every value, so a family of guarded cases must end with an unguarded case of the same pattern. Delete line // 3, and javac says the switch doesn't cover all possible input values, while kotlinc asks you to Add the 'is Book' branch.

You can predict javac's verdict yourself. List the permitted subtypes of the selector's type, and cross off each one that has an unguarded case, or that sits under a sealed parent with one. Inside record patterns, check combinations, not columns. With Pair(Red a, Red b) and Pair(Green a, Light b), the Red cases cover only Red in second place, so Pair(Red, Green) is missing. Whatever is left over is what JDK 27 prints under missing patterns:.

javac also rejects a case that can never be reached, with this case label is dominated by a preceding case label. That happens when an earlier unguarded case already matches everything the later one could. Move line // 3 above line // 1, and javac rejects both guarded lines. Other examples are case String s after case CharSequence cs, and a constant case 1 after an unguarded case Integer i.

kotlinc has no dominance check at all. Put the unguarded is LoanItem.Book first, and it compiles without a warning; every book then gets 21 days, large print and new releases included. Here kotlinc shrugs where javac objects. Kotlin guards (is T if condition) have been stable since Kotlin 2.2.

The sheet is read from the top. Put the most specific rule first, and end each family with an unguarded case.

Several patterns can share one arm only if they bind nothing. On JDK 21 that makes such arms awkward: case Return ret, Renew ren -> fails with illegal fall-through from a pattern, so you write two arms. JDK 22 made unnamed patterns standard, and case Return _, Renew _ -> is legal. _ also stands in for a component you don't need, as in case Borrow(var member, _). On JDK 21 it's a preview feature, one that is switched off unless you pass --enable-preview, and javac stops with unnamed variables are a preview feature and are disabled by default.

The sheet now has the right lines in the right order. What happens when the clerk is handed a blank sheet, or a form that didn't exist when the sheet was printed?

code.title: GuardsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** Cases are tried from the top, and the first one that matches wins. Guards decide the order. */ public class GuardsDemo { enum Format { HARDBACK, PAPERBACK, LARGE_PRINT } sealed interface Item permits Book, Disc {} record Book(Format format, boolean newRelease) implements Item {} record Disc(boolean boxSet) implements Item {} static int loanDays(Item item) { return switch (item) { case Book(var format, var isNew) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42; // 1 case Book(var format, var isNew) when isNew -> 7; // 2 case Book(var format, var isNew) -> 21; // 3 case Disc(var boxSet) when boxSet -> 14; case Disc d -> 7; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { Item[] items = { new Book(Format.LARGE_PRINT, false), new Book(Format.LARGE_PRINT, true), new Book(Format.HARDBACK, true), new Book(Format.PAPERBACK, false), new Disc(true), }; for (Item i : items) { System.out.printf("%-42s %d days%n", i, loanDays(i)); } } }

alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo enum class Format { HARDBACK, PAPERBACK, LARGE_PRINT } sealed interface LoanItem { data class Book(val format: Format, val newRelease: Boolean) : LoanItem data class Disc(val boxSet: Boolean) : LoanItem } // guards in when branches (`is T if condition`) are stable since Kotlin 2.2 fun loanDays(i: LoanItem): Int = when (i) { is LoanItem.Book if i.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42 // 1 is LoanItem.Book if i.newRelease -> 7 // 2 is LoanItem.Book -> 21 // 3 is LoanItem.Disc if i.boxSet -> 14 is LoanItem.Disc -> 7 } /** Branches are tried from the top, and the first one that matches wins. Guards decide the order. */ fun main() { val items = listOf( LoanItem.Book(Format.LARGE_PRINT, false), LoanItem.Book(Format.LARGE_PRINT, true), LoanItem.Book(Format.HARDBACK, true), LoanItem.Book(Format.PAPERBACK, false), LoanItem.Disc(true), ) for (i in items) { println("%-42s %d days".format(i, loanDays(i))) } }

With line 3 on top, javac rejects lines 1 and 2 with this case label is dominated by a preceding case label, while the Kotlin version compiles and gives every book 21 days. Without line 3, javac reports the switch expression does not cover all possible input values and kotlinc asks for the 'is Book' branch. On JDK 22 or newer the preview file prints lend to M-1042, take off the shelf: water damage and not on loan twice; JDK 21 rejects the _.

refs.title: Guard conditions in when expressions (Kotlin docs)

sections.html:
switch has always thrown NullPointerException on a null selector, and a pattern switch keeps that rule unless you opt in with case null. In the picture, a blank sheet handed over the counter stops the clerk, unless the instruction sheet has a line for blank sheets:

Java
return switch (section) {
    case null -> "missing";
    case "FIC" -> "fiction";
    default -> "other";          // default alone does not catch null
};
Kotlin
return when (section) {         // section is a String?
    null -> "missing"
    "FIC" -> "fiction"
    else -> "other"              // without the null branch, null lands here
}

default alone doesn't catch null, and case null, default -> handles both in one arm. For most code, the OpenJDK guide on sealed switches prefers something simpler: reject null before the switch, with Objects.requireNonNull, because a null that reaches the rules is a bug somewhere upstream. Kotlin settles the question in the type system. A when over a nullable subject must handle null somewhere (kotlinc says Add the 'null' branch or an 'else' branch. if it doesn't), and nothing throws. So the NullDemo prints plain(null): NullPointerException in Java and plainWhen(null): other in Kotlin.

Inside a record pattern, null follows a rule that surprises everyone once. A nested record pattern never matches null, but a nested type pattern that covers the whole component type does. Take case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 first and case Line(Point from, Point to) second. A Line whose start is null skips the first case and lands in the second, with from bound to null. Change the second case to Line(Point(var a, var b), Point to), and javac still calls the switch exhaustive. But that Line now matches nothing, and the switch throws MatchException.

That points at the bigger limit: exhaustive is a compile-time promise. javac checks the switch against the subtypes it can see when it compiles. The values it can't see, which the Amber design notes call the remainder, are left to that hidden last arm at run time. The javac/remainder experiment compiles a client against Status permits Active, Closed, a member's account status. Then it recompiles only the hierarchy, with a third status, Frozen, and runs the old client:

active, priority 1
sealed switch: java.lang.MatchException
enum switch:   java.lang.MatchException

The old switch met a status it had never heard of, and the hidden arm threw. An enum switch with no default does the same when it meets a constant added later, and an old Kotlin when throws kotlin.NoWhenBranchMatchedException. You don't write code for the remainder, but in a program that mixes old and new jars, this is the exception you'll see. Recompile the client, and javac turns it back into a compile error, the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, twice.

Exhaustive means exhaustive for the list javac saw. Recompile when the list changes.

In the picture, this is a new kind of form printed after the clerk's sheet was written. Here the picture breaks: a real clerk would ask a colleague. The switch can't ask anyone, so it stops loudly, which beats guessing quietly.

try.title: Feed a switch null, then a stranger
steps: Run NullDemo and NullDemoKt and compare their first lines.

In the Java describe, change case Line(Point from, Point to) to case Line(Point(var a, var b), Point to) (and use a and b in the text). Predict: does it compile? What happens to the line with a null start?
Run the separate-compilation experiment in labs/modernjava/javac/remainder. The five commands are at the top of Client.java.

code.title: NullDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** What a switch does with null: at the top level, and inside a nested pattern. */ public class NullDemo { record Point(int x, int y) {} record Line(Point from, Point to) {} static String plain(String section) { return switch (section) { // the old rule: a null selector throws case "FIC" -> "fiction"; default -> "other"; }; } static String withNull(String section) { return switch (section) { case null -> "missing"; // opt in to null case "FIC" -> "fiction"; default -> "other"; }; } static String nullOrDefault(Object o) { return switch (o) { case String s -> "text " + s; case null, default -> "null or other"; // one arm for both }; } static String describe(Line line) { return switch (line) { case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical"; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "other line " + from + " -> " + to; // Point from also matches null }; } public static void main(String[] args) { try { System.out.println(plain(null)); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("plain(null): NullPointerException"); } System.out.println("withNull(null): " + withNull(null)); System.out.println("nullOrDefault: " + nullOrDefault(null) + " / " + nullOrDefault(42)); System.out.println("line, null start: " + describe(new Line(null, new Point(1, 1)))); } }

alt.title: NullDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo data class Spot(val x: Int, val y: Int) data class Segment(val from: Spot?, val to: Spot?) // in Kotlin the type says whether null can arrive, and when compares with equals: null never throws fun plainWhen(section: String?): String = when (section) { "FIC" -> "fiction" else -> "other" // null lands here } fun withNullWhen(section: String?): String = when (section) { null -> "missing" "FIC" -> "fiction" else -> "other" } fun nullOrElse(o: Any?): String = when (o) { is String -> "text $o" else -> "null or other" } fun describeSegment(s: Segment): String { val from = s.from val to = s.to return when { from != null && to != null && from.x == to.x -> "vertical" else -> "other line $from -> $to" // you write the null case yourself } } /** What when does with null: the nullable type decides, and nothing throws. */ fun main() { println("plainWhen(null): ${plainWhen(null)}") println("withNullWhen(null): ${withNullWhen(null)}") println("nullOrElse: ${nullOrElse(null)} / ${nullOrElse(42)}") println("line, null start: ${describeSegment(Segment(null, Spot(1, 1)))}") }

try.expect: Java prints plain(null): NullPointerException; Kotlin prints plainWhen(null): other, because its when compares with equals and the type allowed null. Both print missing, then null or other twice, then a line whose start is null. After the change in step 2 the switch still compiles, and the null-start line throws java.lang.MatchException. In the experiment, the first run prints active, priority 1, sealed switch: closed and enum switch: priority 2. After only the hierarchy is recompiled, the same old client prints active, priority 1, then sealed switch: java.lang.MatchException and enum switch: java.lang.MatchException. Recompiling the client gives two does not cover all possible input values errors.

compare.title: The loan rules in Java and Kotlin

java.title: LoanRules.java
java.html: static int loanDays(Loan loan) { return switch (loan) { case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42; case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when isNew -> 7; case Loan(var m, Book book, var b) when b == Branch.BUS -> 28; case Loan(var m, Book book, var b) -> 21; case Loan(var m, Disc(var boxSet), var b) when boxSet -> 14; case Loan(var m, Disc disc, var b) -> 7; case Loan(Member(var id, int age), Magazine mag, var b) when age < 12 -> 14; case Loan(Member member, Magazine mag, var b) -> 7; }; }

kotlin.title: LoanRules.kt
kotlin.html: fun loanDays(loan: Loan): Int { val age = loan.member.age return when (val item = loan.item) { is Book if item.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42 is Book if item.newRelease -> 7 is Book if loan.branch == Branch.BUS -> 28 is Book -> 21 is Disc if item.boxSet -> 14 is Disc -> 7 is Magazine if age < 12 -> 14 is Magazine -> 7 } }

compare.note: The rules, the order and the exhaustiveness check are the same in both: the first matching branch wins, guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, and neither version needs a default. The difference is where the data comes apart. Java's record patterns reach into Loan, Member and Book in the label and bind the parts. Kotlin can only test the type of the value it switches on, so the twin pulls item out first, switches on that, and reads loan.member.age and loan.branch by hand. javac also checks dominance, which kotlinc doesn't, and Java's switch has explicit null rules, where Kotlin leaves null to the type system.

worked.title: Rewrite the shelving rules as one switch

steps.say: When an item comes back, this code decides where it goes next. It compiles, it has tests, and it has a bug the compiler can't see. Read it and look for a kind of item it forgets.
steps.code: static String shelveTo(DeskEvent event) { if (event instanceof Returned r) { if (r.item() instanceof Book b) { if (b.newRelease()) return "reservations desk"; return "book trolley"; } if (r.item() instanceof Disc) return "disc shelf"; } return "nowhere"; }

alt.html: fun shelveTo(event: DeskEvent): String { if (event is Returned) { val item = event.item if (item is Book) { if (item.newRelease) return "reservations desk" return "book trolley" } if (item is Disc) return "disc shelf" } return "nowhere" }

steps.say: Name the shapes you care about, most specific first, and let each label take the event apart. DeskEvent is sealed (Returned, Borrowed) and so is Item, so the switch needs no default.
steps.code: static String shelveTo(DeskEvent event) { return switch (event) { // 1. the special case first case Returned(Book(var format, var isNew), int late) when isNew -> "reservations desk"; // 2. then the general cases, one per kind of item case Returned(Book b, int late) -> "book trolley"; case Returned(Disc d, int late) -> "disc shelf"; // 3. events that need no shelving case Borrowed b -> "nowhere"; }; }

alt.html: fun shelveTo(event: DeskEvent): String = when (event) { is Returned -> when (val item = event.item) { // 1. the special case first is Book if item.newRelease -> "reservations desk" // 2. then the general cases, one per kind of item is Book -> "book trolley" is Disc -> "disc shelf" } // 3. events that need no shelving is Borrowed -> "nowhere" }

steps.say: That doesn't compile, in either language: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (kotlinc: Add the 'is Magazine' branch). A returned magazine matches no case. The old chain had the same gap and returned "nowhere", so returned magazines were never put back. The compiler found the bug the tests missed. Add the case.
steps.code: case Returned(Magazine m, int late) -> "reading room"; // the case the chain forgot

alt.html: is Magazine -> "reading room" // the case the chain forgot

steps.say: On JDK 22 or newer, replace the bindings you never use with _, so a reader sees at a glance which parts each rule depends on. Kotlin's version already names only what it reads.
steps.code: // JDK 22+ case Returned(Book(_, var isNew), _) when isNew -> "reservations desk"; case Returned(Book _, _) -> "book trolley"; case Returned(Disc _, _) -> "disc shelf"; case Returned(Magazine _, _) -> "reading room"; case Borrowed _ -> "nowhere";

alt.html: // Kotlin uses _ only for unused lambda parameters and destructured components val (_, daysLate) = returned // skip the item, keep the days late

lab.title: Loan rules over a sealed hierarchy
steps: Run the tests: all eight fail. Read the rule list in the Javadoc of loanDays. The order of the rules is the order of your cases.
Write loanDays as one switch over the Loan, with record patterns and guards and no default. Start with the large-print rule, and run the tests after every two or three cases.
Write label. It needs a case null, and the magazine needs care: what does Magazine(String t) bind when the title is null?
When all eight pass, swap your large-print and new-release cases and run the tests again. Which test catches it? Swap them back.
Delete your last, unguarded book case and compile. Read the error, then put it back.
hints: The first case can be case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42;.
Each kind of item must end with an unguarded case: one for Book, one for Disc, one for Magazine. Otherwise javac says the switch doesn't cover all possible input values.
loanDays doesn't need case null: a pattern switch without one throws NullPointerException, which is what the test expects.

For the child rule, take the member apart too: Loan(Member(var id, int age), Magazine mag, var b) when age < 12. Close the magazine family with the type pattern Member member, which covers every member.
Magazine(String t) matches a magazine whose title is null, with t bound to null. Put case Magazine(String t) when t == null before the general magazine case.

drill.title: A guarded switch from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Given sealed interface Check permits Returned, Damaged, record Returned(int daysLate) and record Damaged(String part, boolean repairable), write nextStep(Check c): items returned 30 or more days late get "send a letter", other returns "reshelve", repairable damage "repair", and other damage "replace". No default. Then write it in Kotlin with when guards.

answer.html: static String nextStep(Check c) { return switch (c) { case Returned(int late) when late >= 30 -> "send a letter"; case Returned r -> "reshelve"; // unguarded: closes the Returned family case Damaged(var part, var repairable) when repairable -> "repair"; case Damaged d -> "replace"; // unguarded: closes the Damaged family }; }

alt.html: fun nextStep(c: Check): String = when (c) { is Check.Returned if c.daysLate >= 30 -> "send a letter" is Check.Returned -> "reshelve" // unguarded: closes the Returned family is Check.Damaged if c.repairable -> "repair" is Check.Damaged -> "replace" // unguarded: closes the Damaged family }

recap: A pattern switch is checked for exhaustiveness and dominance and has fixed null rules. An instanceof chain gets none of that.
Record patterns take records apart in the case label, nested, through the accessors, with var inference and type checks. Kotlin has smart casts and positional destructuring instead.
Cases run top to bottom and the first match wins. Guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, so end each guarded family with an unguarded case. kotlinc doesn't check dominance.
A null selector throws unless you write case null, and default doesn't catch it. A nested type pattern matches a null component; a nested record pattern doesn't.
The limit: exhaustive is a compile-time promise. A subtype or enum constant added later makes an old program throw MatchException (NoWhenBranchMatchedException in Kotlin).
Pattern switch and record patterns are standard from JDK 21, _ from JDK 22, JDK 27 lists the missing patterns, and primitive patterns are still a preview.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "If the switch over our sealed CopyStatus compiles with no default, it can never fail at run time, right?" Explain, in your own words, when it can, and what you would do about each case.
explain.answer: Exhaustive is checked at compile time, against the subtypes javac could see then. At run time two things can still slip through. First, null: a null selector throws NullPointerException unless there is a case null, and a null inside a nested record pattern can make the switch throw MatchException. I'd reject nulls at the edge with Objects.requireNonNull, so they never reach the switch. Second, separate compilation: if the library that defines CopyStatus adds InRepair and our program runs the new jar without being recompiled, the old switch throws MatchException for the new status. The fix is to rebuild against the new version, and then the compiler shows every switch that needs a case. Adding a default to hide it would be worse, because the new status would quietly take the default branch.

deeper.html:
Two newer features build on this lesson. Neither belongs in the labs, which compile for JDK 21.

Primitive types in patterns have been a preview feature in every JDK from 23 to 27, and they are still a preview in the JDK 28 builds. They let a switch over an int use type patterns and guards, and let instanceof ask whether a value fits another primitive type exactly:

Java
// JDK 25: java --enable-preview --source 25 preview/PrimitivePatterns.java
static String length(int pages) {
    return switch (pages) {
        case 0 -> "no pages";
        case int p when p < 100 -> "short (" + p + " pages)";
        case int p -> "medium or long (" + p + " pages)";
    };
}
Kotlin
// Kotlin has always allowed conditions on any subject
fun length(pages: Int): String = when {
    pages == 0 -> "no pages"
    pages < 100 -> "short ($pages pages)"
    else -> "medium or long ($pages pages)"
}

Without the preview flags, JDK 25 stops with primitive patterns are a preview feature and are disabled by default. Treat the syntax as likely to change until it is final.

The second feature is better error messages. JDK 27's javac lists what a non-exhaustive switch is missing, under a missing patterns: line, in the form Rect _ for a type and Pair(Red _,Green _) for a nested record pattern. That one change makes nested exhaustiveness errors much easier to read: on JDK 21 the same Pair switch only says it doesn't cover all possible input values, and you work out the missing combination yourself.

One habit to avoid: don't write case _ when .... JDK 25's javac accepts it, but the language specification doesn't allow it, and a fix in JDK 28 development (JDK-8385488) makes javac reject it. Write default or a real type pattern instead.
